title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Testability Failure (Not Evidence of Safety)
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered independent per‑arm generation would have used up to 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Crucially, this ceiling outcome is a testability failure under the executed semantics (non‑informative for verifier efficacy) — it is not evidence that the LLM+validator pipeline is safe in production. We publish the complete archived run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory test was uninformative, and give concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, exploratory ROC reserves, and pilot checks) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle.

sections.introduction:
Automating human‑intent → device‑configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises to reduce operator burden and accelerate routine NetOps tasks. However, incorrect, misordered, or policy‑violating changes can produce outages and security exposures. One common mitigation is tool‑augmentation: couple an LLM generator with deterministic validators, sandboxed simulators, or constrained executors in a generate–validate–repair pipeline so that proposed changes are checked prior to deployment.

We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) to measure whether deterministic verifier augmentation causally reduces the frequency of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from a hosted LLM under controlled benign and adversarial prompt clusters. The preregistration specified a paired binary estimand (guarded − baseline SAFE rate), an exact McNemar two‑sided test, paired bootstrap CIs (10000 resamples, seed = 1729), N=200 tasks, deterministic task generation, and explicit missingness/exclusion rules. The final, executed run used the declared model gpt‑5‑mini and the deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5. All artifacts (execution and analysis) are archived.

Key outcome and interpretation: under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics the sampled LLM outputs were labeled SAFE by the validator in every confirmatory episode (baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200). This ceiling contingency (n11 = 200) yields an estimated paired difference of 0.0 and p = 1.0. Because identical per‑pair candidates were used and the baseline unsafe rate was zero, the preregistered paired causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The remainder of the paper (1) presents the preregistered run and results; (2) gives an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the test was uninformative; and (3) offers concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations for informative repeats.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and prototype reports document rapid interest in LLMs for NetOps workflows (intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis, limited remediation) while emphasizing safety and evaluation challenges [1,2,3]. Prior work repeatedly advocates tool‑augmentation (generate→validate→refine or divide→verify→refine) and shows task‑dependent correctness gains when external validators or simulators faithfully encode domain constraints [4,1].

Evaluation methodology literature cautions that conclusions about guardrail effectiveness are sensitive to evaluation semantics: how candidate generations are sampled, whether repairs are applied, and whether validation executes in an isolated sandbox with replayable topology/state [5,1]. Red‑teaming and adversarial studies from adjacent domains recommend ROC‑style diagnostics that report both false negatives (missed unsafe proposals) and false positives (false refusals) because operational trade‑offs matter for deployment decisions [2]. Our study adopts these workflow‑centred desiderata (deterministic task generator, sandboxed validation, preregistered estimand and exclusion rules) and targets the empirically identified gap of reproducible adversarial NetOps evaluations with preregistered contrasts between generator‑only and tool‑augmented pipelines.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered as cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on binary SAFE indicators produced by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar (paired_binary_analysis_v1); paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Sampling: N=200 deterministic synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with preregistered seeds; tasks include explicit initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence constraints and were clustered into benign and adversarial prompt transforms.

Pipelines compared. Baseline: accept the LLM candidate and score post hoc with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded: validate the same LLM candidate in a deterministic sandbox using deterministic_netops_validator_v5; repairs were instrumented in the harness but, for confirmatory episodes, repair_provider_trace entries are null (no repairs applied). The validator applies full_intent_constraint_validation and emits deterministic valid flags and violation lists.

Generation semantics and resource accounting. The preregistration allowed two semantics: (A) independent per‑arm generation (one LLM call per arm per task → up to 400 model calls) or (B) shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task shared by both arms → 200 model calls). To conserve model budget the executed run used shared_initial_candidate; execution manifest records model_calls_used = 200 and execution/model_configuration.json declares requested_model = gpt‑5‑mini. Using a shared candidate mechanically limits opportunities for discordant paired outcomes unless the guarded arm modifies the candidate (via repairs) or the validator behaves nondeterministically.

Why the inferential test was uninformative (artifact‑grounded). The inferential degeneracy follows from three archived, reproducible facts: (1) generation semantics — independent_condition_generation = false, i.e., shared_initial_candidate was used (documented in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json); (2) validator outcomes — deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every sampled candidate valid (validation traces in execution/scoring/*.json show validator.valid = true and violation_count = 0); and (3) repairs were not exercised — repair_provider_trace fields are null across confirmatory scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json). Because both arms scored the identical candidate and no repair changed guarded outputs, there was no arm‑level variation to produce discordant pairs; therefore the McNemar contrast is mechanically untestable. The analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg) reproduce the degenerate contingency and statistical outputs.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The execution manifest reports completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json). Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200; deterministic reconciliation checks passed.

Confirmatory contingency and statistics. The deterministic validator produced SAFE labels for every confirmatory episode: baseline SAFE = 200/200 and guarded SAFE = 200/200. The paired contingency is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). From these counts the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0. Paired_binary_analysis_v1 reports exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729); all numerical outputs are archived in analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv.

Representative traces and repair instrumentation. Representative scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑00000X‑*.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content across baseline and guarded episodes, validator.valid = true, violation_count = 0, and repair_provider_trace = null. These traces confirm that the guarded pipeline performed only deterministic validation and did not change candidates in the confirmatory episodes; no UNSAFE→SAFE conversions via automatic repair occurred in the archived confirmatory set.

Exploratory reserves and missingness. The preregistration reserved up to 50 exploratory tasks to estimate verifier ROC and refusal trade‑offs; that reserve was not consumed prior to confirmatory execution. Missingness and contamination artifacts report complete_pairs = 200 and no flagged episodes (analysis/missingness_summary.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The ceiling contingency (n11 = 200) should not be read as evidence that the LLM plus deterministic validator guarantees safety in broader contexts. Instead, it documents that under the executed shared generation semantics the confirmatory contrast could not produce discordant outcomes: identical per‑pair candidates were scored identically, and no repair mechanism or validator nondeterminism introduced arm‑level divergence. The preregistered power calculation (which assumed a baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15% and nonzero discordant proportions) therefore did not apply to the executed semantics or sampled model behaviour.

Design implications and concrete recommendations (artifact‑supported). All recommendations map directly to archived manifest and analysis artifacts:
- Adopt independent per‑arm generation for paired causal contrasts unless the guarded arm reliably applies deterministic repairs that change candidates. Independent draws require ≈200 additional model calls for N=200 (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 vs executed model_calls_used = 200; execution/execution_manifest.json).
- Use the preregistered exploratory reserve to calibrate adversarial transforms until the baseline unsafe rate matches power assumptions. Archive those calibration runs and fix transform parameters before the confirmatory set to preserve preregistration integrity.
- Instrument and archive repair_provider_trace artifacts; quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions and any repair‑introduced regressions before treating repairs as part of the guarded effect.
- Run a small deterministic pilot and inspect contingency counts; if the pilot produces a ceiling/floor contingency, follow preregistered contingency‑preserving remediation paths (enable independent draws, strengthen adversarial transforms) rather than proceeding to an uninformative confirmatory test.

Threats to validity and generality. Construct validity: the synthetic tasks constrained fields (admin, mtu, vlan) and single‑AS topologies; validator completeness relative to production failure modes is limited. External validity: the run evaluated a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) in synthetic sandboxes; no claims of production readiness or cross‑model generality are made. Internal validity: the executed semantics (shared_initial_candidate) are the proximate cause of testability failure. Conclusion validity: lack of discordant pairs prevents inference about verifier effect; the p = 1.0 and degenerate CI reflect this mechanical constraint rather than evidence of equivalence in broader settings.

Operational implications. For operator decision‑making, the resource trade‑off between independent generation (more model calls) and testability must be explicit: archived execution manifests make the per‑task call accounting reproducible so operators can weight call costs against inferential informativeness. Strict guardrails may still be valuable in deployment but require ROC‑style calibration (refusal vs false‑negative trade‑offs) on domain‑appropriate adversarial datasets prior to rollout.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt‑5‑mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and repairs were not exercised, the preregistered paired causal hypothesis was untestable in this run. This outcome is a testability failure and should not be interpreted as evidence of verifier effectiveness or operational safety. The scientific contribution is therefore reproducibility‑centred and methodological: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts enabling deterministic replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial calibration using exploratory reserves, repair instrumentation, and pilot checks) to enable informative repeats. Investigators planning repeats should consult the archived execution and analysis artifacts before changing preregistered design choices; those artifacts precisely document the generation semantics, model call accounting, validator traces, and statistical parameters used here.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
